subject: Accounting
title: Net Income: The Bottom Line
description: One-minute skill: Net Income: The Bottom Line.

hook.text: After all revenues, costs, taxes, and interest—one number remains. Net income.

buildup.text: Net income is the final profit. It's what flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet.

discovery.text: Investors divide it by shares outstanding to get earnings per share—Wall Street's favorite metric.

twist.text: Net income can be manipulated through timing tricks, one-time charges, and creative accounting.

climax.text: Smart analysts never rely on net income alone—they dig deeper into cash flow and quality.

punchline.text: The bottom line matters. But check what's under it.

quiz.question: What does net income represent?
options: Final profit after all expenses and taxes

details.summary: Net income—the 'bottom line'—is the profit remaining after all expenses, taxes, and interest are subtracted from revenue. This topic explains how net income is calculated, what it includes, and why it doesn't always reflect the economic reality of a business.
details.whyItMatters: Net income is the most widely reported profit measure, but it includes non-cash items and one-time charges that can make it misleading. Understanding its components is essential for proper interpretation.
takeaways: Net income equals revenue minus all expenses including COGS, operating expenses, interest, and taxes
Non-cash expenses like depreciation reduce net income without affecting actual cash flow
One-time charges or gains can distort net income, making trend analysis unreliable without adjustments

faq.question: What exactly is net income and why does it matter?
faq.answer: Net income is the total profit remaining after subtracting all expenses—cost of goods sold, operating expenses, interest, taxes, and any other charges—from total revenue. It appears at the bottom of the income statement and is used to calculate earnings per share.

faq.question: Why might net income be misleading?
faq.answer: Net income includes non-cash charges like depreciation and amortization, one-time items like restructuring charges or asset sales, and is affected by accounting policy choices. A company can report strong net income while generating weak or negative cash flow.
